cues.text: A Duke's Grandson, A Pope's Great-Grandson

Francis Borgia was born in 1510 into a family whose fortunes were as spectacular as its reputation was troubled: his great-grandfather on his father's side was Pope Alexander VI, and his mother's grandfather was King Ferdinand of Aragon.

Raised at the court of Emperor Charles V, he married Eleanor de Castro, a Portuguese noblewoman, at nineteen, and the couple went on to have eight children while Francis rose through the highest ranks of Spanish public life.

In 1539 the emperor made him viceroy of Catalonia, where he pursued genuine reforms — clearing Barcelona's streets of banditry, appointing fair judges, and giving generously to the poor — before succeeding his father as Duke of Gandia in 1543.
A Coffin and a Conversion
In 1539 Francis was assigned the grim duty of escorting the body of the Empress Isabella to its final resting place at Granada.
As protocol required, he had to formally identify her remains before burial—remains so disfigured by the journey's heat and delay that the beautiful empress he had known was unrecognizable.
The experience is traditionally said to have moved him to a private vow never again to serve a master who could suffer such a fate.
It is also traditionally said to have moved him to give himself instead to God alone, though he continued fulfilling his public duties for years afterward.
When his wife Eleanor died in 1546, Francis judged the moment had come: he provided for his children's futures, secured the succession of his duchy, and in 1550 traveled to Rome, where St.
Ignatius of Loyola personally received him into the young Society of Jesus.
The Second Founder

Ordained a priest in 1551, Francis spent the following years as a parish priest and then as the Jesuits' commissary general for Spain and Portugal, before being elected the order's third Superior General in 1565.
Under his leadership the Society expanded with striking speed across Europe and into the missions of Asia and the Americas.
Francis wrote much of the internal structure — rules governing spiritual formation, study, and discipline — that gave the growing order its lasting shape.
His reforms were substantial enough that historians of the Jesuits have long called him their second founder.
The title was earned less by any single dramatic achievement than by the patient, administrative labor.
This patient, administrative labor turned a fast-growing movement into an institution that could outlast its founders.
A Final Mission and a Quiet Death

In 1571, already past sixty and in declining health, Francis undertook one last diplomatic mission at the pope's request, traveling to Spain, Portugal, and France to help build a Christian alliance against Ottoman advances in the Mediterranean.

The journey broke what strength remained to him; he fell seriously ill on the road home and reached Rome only at the end of September 1572, dying there within days, on the 30th, at the age of sixty-one.
Legacy
Pope Clement X canonized Francis Borgia in 1671, a century after his death, closing the circle on his life.
That life began amid one of the Church's most notorious family names.
It ended in a humility so complete that popes who wished to make him a cardinal could never persuade him to accept.
We recognize in Francis a witness to the truth that inherited privilege, however tainted its origins, does not determine what a soul becomes.
We recognize that a man born to the Borgia name could still choose, deliberately and repeatedly across a whole lifetime, to set that inheritance aside for something worth infinitely more.
